Hepatic failure and renal failure.

name: BLEMANGO-5G
sourceDescription: Omega-3 Fatty Acids,Ginkgo Biloba Extract, Ginseng Extract, Green Tea Extract, Grape Seed Extract, Multimineral Multivitamin with Antioxidants & Trace Elements Soft Gelatin Capsules
displayDescription: Omega-3 fatty acids, botanical extracts, multivitamins, multiminerals, antioxidants and trace elements soft-gel capsules

clinical.summary: Ramnova soft gelatin capsule listed as omega-3 fatty acids with ginkgo biloba, ginseng, green tea and grape seed extracts, plus unenumerated multimineral, multivitamin, antioxidant and trace element blends. No strength is stated for any ingredient and the blends are not itemised, so no dose-dependent statement can be made about this product. United States evidence reviews for the named botanicals do not establish a use for any of them, and two of them carry safety signals that matter in a capsule: green tea extract has been linked to liver injury, and ginkgo may increase bleeding risk. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health states that there is no conclusive evidence that ginkgo is helpful for any health condition. A trial in more than 3,000 people aged 75 or older found no difference from placebo in the rate of developing dementia over a median of about six years.
The same body states that definite conclusions cannot yet be reached on whether green tea is helpful for most of the purposes for which it is used.
For Asian ginseng, the evidence is limited and mixed; a 2023 review suggested a possible effect on general fatigue, and most research shows it does not improve athletic performance.

For grape seed extract, reviews suggest possible effects on LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and diastolic blood pressure, but the evidence is not sufficient to conclude it is helpful for wound healing or tooth decay.
UK labelling for omega-3-acid ethyl esters covers endogenous hypertriglyceridaemia as a supplement to diet, which is a prescription indication at gram doses and not a general nutritional use.
No source reviewed here establishes a use for this product or for this combination of ingredients.
sideEffects: Reported effects of ginkgo leaf extract are dizziness, gastrointestinal symptoms and headache.
Reported effects of green tea are nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort and increased blood pressure.
Insomnia is described as the most common side effect of Asian ginseng; severe rash, liver damage and allergic reactions have also been reported.
Grape seed extract is described as generally well tolerated when taken orally.
Common gastrointestinal effects of omega-3-acid ethyl esters include abdominal distension, abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, dyspepsia, flatulence, eructation, nausea and vomiting.
warnings: Liver injury has been reported in people who used green tea products, primarily green tea extracts in tablet or capsule form. People with a particular gene variant, present in between 5 and 15 per cent of Americans, appear especially susceptible. This product is a capsule containing green tea extract, so the form implicated in those reports is the form used here.
Ginkgo may increase the risk of bleeding in people taking anticoagulant drugs such as warfarin.

This product contains both ginkgo and omega-3 fatty acids. Ginkgo is associated with increased bleeding risk, and omega-3-acid ethyl ester labelling describes a moderate increase in bleeding time at 4 g daily. No source reviewed here quantifies the combined effect, and neither amount is stated for this product.
Green tea contains caffeine. Caffeine intake should not exceed moderate levels in pregnancy, and high caffeine intake while breastfeeding can cause fussiness and poor sleep patterns in infants.

Asian ginseng appears safe for short-term use of up to six months, but questions have been raised about its long-term safety. It is not recommended during pregnancy, because one of its constituents has been found to cause birth defects in animals, and its safety while breastfeeding is unknown.
The safety of grape seed extract during pregnancy and breastfeeding is not known.

Licensed omega-3-acid ethyl ester labelling describes a dose-dependent increased risk of atrial fibrillation in patients with established cardiovascular disease or cardiovascular risk factors at 4 g daily, and advises caution in patients with known sensitivity to fish. The omega-3 amount in this product is not stated, so no source reviewed here characterises that risk here.
contraindications: No contraindication is established for this product by any source reviewed here. The botanical reviews cited are evidence summaries rather than regulatory labelling and do not carry contraindication sections, and the composition of this product is not sufficiently specified to map regulatory contraindications onto it.
interactions: Ginkgo may increase the risk of bleeding in people taking anticoagulant drugs such as warfarin.
Green tea is reported to interact with nadolol, atorvastatin and raloxifene.
Prothrombin time must be checked when omega-3-acid ethyl esters are combined with warfarin, or when such treatment is stopped.

No specific drug interaction is named in the cited reviews for Asian ginseng or grape seed extract; both reviews advise anyone taking medicines to consult a health professional before use, because some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.
clinical.scopeNote: Assembled from four United States evidence reviews for the named botanicals and one UK Summary of Product Characteristics for a licensed omega-3 medicine, because no Indian pack insert, CDSCO approval or Indian peer-reviewed source for BLEMANGO-5G was located. The gaps here are larger than the coverage. Four of the nine listed ingredients are blends, described in the source catalogue only as multimineral, multivitamin, antioxidant and trace elements, and their members are not enumerated anywhere reviewed here; the product record flags this. No strength is stated for any of the nine, so nothing above can be read as a dose, and no statement can be made about total vitamin or mineral intake, about upper intake levels, or about the standardisation of any botanical extract. The botanical reviews cited are general evidence and safety summaries about each plant; they do not correspond to any particular extract, standardisation, preparation or dose, and they are not regulatory labelling for this or any product. The omega-3 source is a 1000 mg prescription capsule licensed for hypertriglyceridaemia at 2 to 4 capsules daily, and its statements about bleeding time and atrial fibrillation are characterised at 4 g daily; they are reproduced as labelled context for the ingredient, not as risks established at whatever amount this product contains, and the source does not establish which fatty acids or esters are present here. The bleeding-risk overlap between the ginkgo and the omega-3 in this same capsule is flagged above but is not quantified by any source reviewed here. The catalogue therapy category, nutritional support, is itself marked as inferred from composition rather than sourced. Nothing above verifies the India-approved status, composition, strengths, dosing or pack insert of BLEMANGO-5G.

name: BLEMANGO SYRUP
displayDescription: Multivitamin, multimineral and astaxanthin syrup

clinical.summary: Ramnova syrup listed as a multivitamin and multimineral preparation with astaxanthin. The vitamin and mineral blends are not itemised and no strength is stated for any ingredient, including the astaxanthin, so almost nothing can be said about this product from the sources reviewed. The one substantive point available is that a European Food Safety Authority opinion on astaxanthin in food supplements found that combined exposure exceeds the acceptable daily intake for children and reaches it for adolescents. That matters for a syrup, because syrups are a presentation commonly given to children, but the astaxanthin amount here is not stated. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
warnings: The European Food Safety Authority established an acceptable daily intake for astaxanthin of 0.2 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, derived by applying an uncertainty factor of 200 to a lowest observed adverse effect level of 40 mg per kilogram of body weight per day from a two-year rat study.

Assessing astaxanthin as a novel food in supplements at up to 8 mg per day, the same opinion concluded that combined exposure from the diet plus supplements was below the acceptable daily intake for adults, reached it for adolescents aged 14 to 18, exceeded it by about 28 per cent for children aged 10 to 14, and exceeded it more substantially for children under 10.

Because neither the astaxanthin amount nor an intended age group is stated for this product, no source reviewed here establishes whether its astaxanthin content falls within the acceptable daily intake for any particular person, and this is the specific question a reviewer should resolve from the pack.
clinical.scopeNote: Only one source is cited, a European Food Safety Authority safety opinion on astaxanthin used as a novel food in food supplements, because no Indian pack insert, CDSCO approval or Indian peer-reviewed source for BLEMANGO SYRUP was located, and the rest of the composition cannot be sourced at all as stated. The multivitamin and multimineral components are described in the source catalogue only by those words, with no members and no amounts, and the product record flags that the full blend composition and strengths are not supplied; without an itemised composition no vitamin or mineral can be checked against a recommended intake or an upper intake level, and no claim is made about any of them here. The astaxanthin amount is likewise not stated. The uses, side effects, contraindications and interactions lists are deliberately empty: the cited opinion is a safety assessment of intake levels, not an efficacy review and not a regulatory label, so it establishes no therapeutic use, no adverse reaction profile and no interaction for astaxanthin or for this product. The acceptable daily intake figures above are quoted for the ingredient at the supplement levels EFSA assessed and are not statements about this product's content. EFSA's assessment also concerns a specific novel food form of astaxanthin, derived from Haematococcus pluvialis, and no source reviewed here establishes which form is used here. The catalogue therapy category, nutritional support, is itself marked as inferred from composition rather than sourced. Nothing above verifies the India-approved status, composition, strengths, intended age group, dosing or pack insert of BLEMANGO SYRUP.

clinical.summary: Ramnova tablet listed as calcium carbonate with vitamin D3 250 I.U. No Indian pack insert or CDSCO approval for this product was located, so the outline below is drawn from the UK Summary of Product Characteristics for a licensed calcium carbonate and colecalciferol tablet. That source product is a much higher strength than the vitamin D content listed here, and the calcium content of this product is not stated at all. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: UK labelling for a calcium carbonate and colecalciferol tablet covers use as an adjunct to specific therapy for osteoporosis, and situations requiring therapeutic supplementation such as pregnancy and established vitamin D dependent osteomalacia.
The same labelling covers the prevention and treatment of calcium and vitamin D deficiency, particularly in housebound and institutionalised elderly people.

Hypercalciuria and, with prolonged high doses, hypercalcaemia may occur.
Hypersensitivity reactions including pruritus, wheezing and urticaria have been reported.
warnings: Serum and urinary calcium should be monitored during long-term treatment, and treatment reviewed if hypercalcaemia or signs of impaired renal function appear.
Care is needed in patients with renal impairment, and in patients with a history of renal stones or severe hypercalciuria.
Additional calcium or vitamin D from other medicines, supplements or fortified foods should be taken into account, because the total intake is what determines the risk of hypercalcaemia.
Osteoporosis arising from immobilisation is a relative contraindication in the source labelling, because immobilised patients are more exposed to hypercalcaemia.
contraindications: Hypercalcaemia, including hypercalcaemia resulting from myeloma, bone metastases or other malignant bone disease, and from sarcoidosis.
Primary hyperparathyroidism.
Vitamin D overdosage, or existing vitamin D toxicity.
Severe renal failure.
Hypersensitivity to the active substances.
interactions: Thiazide diuretics reduce urinary calcium excretion and increase the risk of hypercalcaemia.
The effects of cardiac glycosides such as digitalis may be accentuated by a rise in serum calcium, and cardiac arrhythmias may result.

Calcium salts reduce the absorption of levothyroxine, bisphosphonates, sodium fluoride, quinolone antibiotics, tetracycline antibiotics, zinc, strontium ranelate and iron. The source labelling advises allowing a minimum of four hours before taking the calcium.
Phenytoin and barbiturates reduce the effect of vitamin D.
Foods containing oxalic acid or phytic acid may reduce calcium absorption.

clinical.summary: Ramnova tablet listed as calcium citrate with vitamin D, methylcobalamin, magnesium, zinc, folic acid and pyridoxine hydrochloride. The product listing gives no strength for any of the seven ingredients, so no dose-dependent statement can be made about it. No Indian pack insert or CDSCO approval for this combination was located. The outline below is drawn from UK Summaries of Product Characteristics for licensed products covering only part of this composition. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: UK labelling for a licensed calcium and colecalciferol tablet covers use as an adjunct to specific therapy for osteoporosis, therapeutic supplementation in malnutrition, and the prevention and treatment of calcium and vitamin D deficiency.
UK labelling for oral cyanocobalamin covers the treatment of nutritional vitamin B12 deficiency and of vitamin B12 deficiency following partial gastrectomy.

UK labelling for folic acid covers the treatment of megaloblastic anaemia due to folic acid deficiency, and prophylaxis in chronic haemolytic states, renal dialysis and drug-induced folate deficiency.
sideEffects: Gastrointestinal disturbances have been reported with calcium and vitamin D tablets, and hypercalciuria and hypercalcaemia may occur with prolonged high doses.
Gastrointestinal effects reported with folic acid include abdominal distension, flatulence, anorexia and nausea.
Allergic reactions to folic acid are rare and include erythema, rash, urticaria, dyspnoea and anaphylaxis.
Sensitisation to cyanocobalamin is rare and may present as an itching exanthema, and exceptionally as anaphylactic shock.
warnings: Serum and urinary calcium should be monitored during long-term calcium and vitamin D treatment, with care in renal impairment and in patients with a history of renal stones or severe hypercalciuria.

Folic acid must not be given for pernicious anaemia or undiagnosed megaloblastic anaemia without sufficient vitamin B12, because folic acid alone may precipitate subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. This product contains both folic acid and methylcobalamin, but neither amount is stated, so no source reviewed here establishes whether the vitamin B12 content is sufficient for that purpose.
Caution is required with folic acid in patients with folate-dependent tumours.

Where vitamin B12 is used in pernicious anaemia, the source labelling requires an adequate dose and regular examination of the blood picture, at least every three months for 18 months until stabilised and annually thereafter. It also warns that indiscriminate administration of vitamin B12 may mask a precise diagnosis.

This product combines calcium with zinc in a single tablet. Calcium salts reduce the absorption of zinc, and folic acid may also reduce intestinal absorption of zinc; no source reviewed here quantifies the net effect for this formulation.
contraindications: Hypercalcaemia, including hypercalcaemia resulting from myeloma, bone metastases or other malignant bone disease, and from sarcoidosis.
Primary hyperparathyroidism.
Vitamin D overdosage, or existing vitamin D toxicity.
Severe renal failure.
For the folic acid component, malignant disease, unless there is megaloblastic anaemia due to folic acid deficiency.
Hypersensitivity to any of the active substances.
interactions: Thiazide diuretics reduce urinary calcium excretion and increase the risk of hypercalcaemia.
The effects of cardiac glycosides such as digitalis may be accentuated by a rise in serum calcium, and cardiac arrhythmias may result.

Calcium salts reduce the absorption of levothyroxine, bisphosphonates, sodium fluoride, quinolone antibiotics, tetracycline antibiotics, zinc, strontium ranelate and iron, and the source labelling advises a minimum of four hours before taking the calcium.
Phenytoin and barbiturates reduce the effect of vitamin D.
Sulfasalazine and cholestyramine reduce folic acid absorption, and antacids reduce it unless dosing is separated by at least two hours.
Trimethoprim and sulfonamides reduce the effectiveness of folic acid, and serum levels of phenytoin, phenobarbital and primidone may be reduced by folic acid.

Absorption of vitamin B12 may be reduced by para-aminosalicylic acid, colchicine, biguanides such as metformin, neomycin, cholestyramine, potassium chloride, methyldopa and cimetidine. Patients taking chloramphenicol may respond poorly.

displayDescription: Esomeprazole 40 mg and domperidone 30 mg sustained-release capsules

clinical.summary: Ramnova sustained-release capsule containing esomeprazole and domperidone. No combination-product licence was located in a major regulatory jurisdiction, so the outline below is drawn from the UK Summary of Product Characteristics for each ingredient separately. Note that UK labelling for domperidone covers only the relief of nausea and vomiting, limits adults to 30 mg per day, and limits treatment to a maximum of one week. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: UK labelling for esomeprazole covers erosive reflux oesophagitis, maintenance of healed oesophagitis to prevent relapse, and symptomatic treatment of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

UK labelling for esomeprazole also covers eradication of Helicobacter pylori in combination with appropriate antibacterial therapy, healing of Helicobacter pylori associated duodenal ulcer, and prevention of relapse of peptic ulcers in patients with Helicobacter pylori associated ulcers.

UK labelling for esomeprazole further covers healing of gastric ulcers associated with NSAID therapy, prevention of gastric and duodenal ulcers associated with NSAID therapy in patients at risk, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
UK labelling for domperidone covers only the relief of the symptoms of nausea and vomiting. Indications relating to dyspepsia, heartburn and reflux were not present in the labelling reviewed.
sideEffects: Common with esomeprazole are headache, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, constipation, flatulence and benign fundic gland polyps.

Severe hypomagnesaemia has been reported in patients treated with proton pump inhibitors for at least three months, and may present as fatigue, tetany, delirium, convulsions, dizziness or ventricular arrhythmia.

Proton pump inhibitors are associated with very infrequent cases of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and very rarely with erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms.
Common with domperidone are somnolence and headache.
Domperidone has been associated with prolongation of the QT interval and with rare cases of torsades de pointes.
warnings: In the presence of alarm symptoms such as significant unintentional weight loss, recurrent vomiting, dysphagia, haematemesis or melaena, gastric malignancy should be excluded before treatment, because treatment with esomeprazole may relieve symptoms and delay diagnosis.
Treatment with a proton pump inhibitor at high doses and over long durations, longer than one year, may modestly increase the risk of hip, wrist and spine fracture, predominantly in the elderly.

Epidemiological studies showed that domperidone was associated with an increased risk of serious ventricular arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death. The risk is higher in patients older than 60 years, at daily doses above 30 mg, and with concurrent QT-prolonging medicines or potent CYP3A4 inhibitors.

UK labelling limits adults to a maximum domperidone dose of 30 mg per day and states that the maximum treatment duration should not exceed one week. This product delivers 30 mg of domperidone, which is at that maximum daily dose.

Treatment with a proton pump inhibitor should be discontinued if lesions arise in sun-exposed areas of skin accompanied by arthralgia, and medical attention sought promptly, because this may indicate subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus.

Long-term proton pump inhibitor treatment may reduce the absorption of vitamin B12 as a consequence of reduced gastric acid, and may slightly increase the risk of gastrointestinal infections caused by bacteria.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to esomeprazole, to domperidone, to substituted benzimidazoles, or to any of the excipients.
Concomitant use of esomeprazole with nelfinavir.
Confirmed or suspected phaeochromocytoma, or a prolactin-releasing pituitary tumour.
Gastrointestinal haemorrhage, mechanical obstruction or perforation.
Moderate or severe hepatic impairment.
Known existing prolongation of the QTc interval, significant electrolyte disturbances, or underlying cardiac disease such as congestive heart failure.
Concomitant use with QT-prolonging medicines, other than apomorphine under the specific conditions set out in its own labelling.
Concomitant use with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, regardless of their QT-prolonging effects.
interactions: Concomitant use of esomeprazole with clopidogrel reduces exposure to the active metabolite of clopidogrel by about 40 per cent, and the combination is discouraged.
Esomeprazole should not be co-administered with atazanavir, because exposure to atazanavir is substantially reduced. Co-administration with nelfinavir is contraindicated.
Esomeprazole increases the bioavailability of digoxin by approximately 10 to 30 per cent, and reinforced monitoring is recommended at high doses.
Esomeprazole may elevate serum methotrexate levels; temporary withdrawal of the proton pump inhibitor may be considered during high-dose methotrexate therapy.
Esomeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 and may increase plasma concentrations of diazepam, phenytoin and citalopram, which may require dose adjustment.

Concomitant use of domperidone with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, including HIV protease inhibitors, systemic azole antifungals such as ketoconazole, and macrolides such as erythromycin, is contraindicated. Marked interaction with ketoconazole or erythromycin produced mean QTc prolongation of approximately 10 milliseconds.
Concomitant use of domperidone with other QT-prolonging medicines is contraindicated, with the specific exception of apomorphine used under the precautions set out in its own labelling.
clinical.scopeNote: Assembled from two single-ingredient UK Summaries of Product Characteristics because no combination licence was located in a major jurisdiction. The domperidone source describes a 10 mg orodispersible immediate-release tablet, not the 30 mg sustained-release presentation in this product, and its labelled indication is limited to the relief of nausea and vomiting with a maximum of 30 mg per day for no longer than one week. Those dose and duration limits, and the cardiac contraindications attached to them, were set for that presentation and have not been shown here to apply unchanged to a sustained-release combination intended for longer use alongside a proton pump inhibitor. The esomeprazole source describes a 40 mg gastro-resistant capsule, matching the strength in this product. Nothing above verifies ESORUSK-D's India-approved indication, its pack insert, the clinical effect of the specific 40 mg / 30 mg SR combination, or the cardiac safety of that combination.

clinical.summary: Ramnova sustained-release capsule containing esomeprazole and levosulpiride. No combination-product licence was located in a major regulatory jurisdiction. The esomeprazole outline below is drawn from the UK Summary of Product Characteristics. No UK or US licensed product information was located for levosulpiride, so the entries for that component are drawn from published Indian clinical studies rather than from approved labelling. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: UK labelling for esomeprazole covers erosive reflux oesophagitis, maintenance of healed oesophagitis to prevent relapse, and symptomatic treatment of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

UK labelling for esomeprazole also covers eradication of Helicobacter pylori in combination with appropriate antibacterial therapy, healing of Helicobacter pylori associated duodenal ulcer, and prevention of relapse of peptic ulcers in patients with Helicobacter pylori associated ulcers.

UK labelling for esomeprazole further covers healing of gastric ulcers associated with NSAID therapy, prevention of gastric and duodenal ulcers associated with NSAID therapy in patients at risk, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

No approved indication for levosulpiride was located in UK or US labelling. Published Indian clinical literature describes it as a substituted benzamide used increasingly for gastric motility disorders, and commonly prescribed alongside proton pump inhibitors.
sideEffects: Common with esomeprazole are headache, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, constipation, flatulence and benign fundic gland polyps.

Severe hypomagnesaemia has been reported in patients treated with proton pump inhibitors for at least three months, and may present as fatigue, tetany, delirium, convulsions, dizziness or ventricular arrhythmia.

Proton pump inhibitors are associated with very infrequent cases of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and very rarely with erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms.

Levosulpiride has been associated with movement disorders. In a prospective study of 30 patients at an Indian tertiary care centre, 86.66 per cent presented with stiffness, tremor or both; reported features included resting tremor, rigidity, dystonia, dysarthria, abnormal gait, and neck or back pain with muscle spasm.

Levosulpiride raises serum prolactin. A published Indian case report describes a patient taking levosulpiride sustained release 75 mg who developed a serum prolactin of 273 nanograms per millilitre against a reference range of 3.7 to 17.9, with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea; the authors note that a significant number of patients who use levosulpiride develop levels above 200 nanograms per millilitre, and cite a study reporting galactorrhoea in 26.7 per cent of patients.
warnings: In the presence of alarm symptoms such as significant unintentional weight loss, recurrent vomiting, dysphagia, haematemesis or melaena, gastric malignancy should be excluded before treatment, because treatment with esomeprazole may relieve symptoms and delay diagnosis.
Treatment with a proton pump inhibitor at high doses and over long durations, longer than one year, may modestly increase the risk of hip, wrist and spine fracture, predominantly in the elderly.

Levosulpiride-induced movement disorders became more frequent with longer treatment. In the Indian study cited, onset ranged from four days to more than six months, most patients presented after three to five weeks, and a statistically significant positive correlation was found between treatment duration and the incidence of tremor and stiffness.

The authors of that study advise that levosulpiride should be considered as a possible cause of acute recent-onset extrapyramidal syndromes, and that early recognition is essential for complete recovery.
In the prolactin case reported, serum prolactin fell and menstruation resumed within one to two weeks of stopping levosulpiride, which indicates that the effect may be reversible on withdrawal.

Treatment with a proton pump inhibitor should be discontinued if lesions arise in sun-exposed areas of skin accompanied by arthralgia, and long-term treatment may reduce the absorption of vitamin B12.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to esomeprazole, to levosulpiride, to substituted benzimidazoles, or to any of the excipients.
Concomitant use of esomeprazole with nelfinavir.

No licensed contraindication list was located for levosulpiride in a major regulatory jurisdiction. The absence of a listed set of contraindications is not evidence that none apply, and the pack insert should be consulted.
interactions: Concomitant use of esomeprazole with clopidogrel reduces exposure to the active metabolite of clopidogrel by about 40 per cent, and the combination is discouraged.
Esomeprazole should not be co-administered with atazanavir, because exposure to atazanavir is substantially reduced. Co-administration with nelfinavir is contraindicated.
Esomeprazole increases the bioavailability of digoxin by approximately 10 to 30 per cent, and reinforced monitoring is recommended at high doses.
Esomeprazole may elevate serum methotrexate levels; temporary withdrawal of the proton pump inhibitor may be considered during high-dose methotrexate therapy.
Esomeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 and may increase plasma concentrations of diazepam, phenytoin and citalopram, which may require dose adjustment.

No licensed interaction profile was located for levosulpiride in a major regulatory jurisdiction. Because levosulpiride acts as a dopamine D2 antagonist, the pack insert should be consulted before use with other dopamine antagonists or with dopaminergic medicines.
clinical.scopeNote: No combination licence was located in a major jurisdiction. The esomeprazole entries come from a UK Summary of Product Characteristics for a 40 mg gastro-resistant capsule, matching the strength in this product. Levosulpiride holds no UK or US marketing authorisation, so no approved labelling exists for it; the entries above are drawn from two peer-reviewed Indian publications, one a prospective single-centre study of 30 patients and the other a single case report with a literature discussion. Those are observational reports of harm rather than regulatory labelling, and they do not constitute a complete adverse-effect, contraindication or interaction profile. The prolactin case report concerns levosulpiride sustained release 75 mg, which matches the levosulpiride strength in this product. Nothing above verifies ESORUSK-LS's India-approved indication, its pack insert, or the clinical effect of the specific 40 mg / 75 mg SR combination.

name: KRUJOCET-M
displayDescription: Levocetirizine 5 mg and montelukast 10 mg tablets

clinical.summary: Ramnova combination tablet containing levocetirizine and montelukast. No combination-product licence was located in a major regulatory jurisdiction, so the outline below is drawn from the UK Summary of Product Characteristics for each ingredient separately. Note that UK labelling positions montelukast as add-on therapy in asthma rather than as a treatment for allergic rhinitis on its own. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: UK labelling for levocetirizine covers the symptomatic treatment of allergic rhinitis, including persistent allergic rhinitis, and urticaria, in adults and children aged 6 years and above.

UK labelling for montelukast covers the treatment of mild to moderate persistent asthma as add-on therapy in patients inadequately controlled on inhaled corticosteroids alone, and the prevention of exercise-induced bronchoconstriction in patients with asthma.

UK labelling for montelukast states that, in asthmatic patients, it can also provide symptomatic relief of seasonal allergic rhinitis. It is not labelled as a treatment for allergic rhinitis in patients without asthma.
sideEffects: Common with levocetirizine are somnolence, reported in 5.2 per cent of patients, headache in 2.6 per cent, dry mouth in 2.6 per cent, and fatigue in 2.5 per cent.
Common with montelukast are headache, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, rash, elevated serum transaminases and pyrexia.

Uncommon neuropsychiatric reactions to montelukast include abnormal dreams such as nightmares, insomnia, sleepwalking, anxiety, agitation including aggressive behaviour or hostility, depression and psychomotor hyperactivity.

Rare neuropsychiatric reactions to montelukast include disturbance in attention, memory impairment and tic. Very rare reactions include hallucinations, disorientation, suicidal thinking and behaviour, and obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
Pruritus may occur when levocetirizine is stopped, even if that symptom was not present before treatment.
warnings: The US Food and Drug Administration requires a boxed warning, its most prominent warning, on montelukast prescribing information describing serious mental health side effects. A wide variety of mental health side effects have been reported, including completed suicides.

In the same 2020 communication, the US Food and Drug Administration advised that montelukast should only be prescribed for allergic rhinitis in patients who have an inadequate response or intolerance to alternative therapies. This is directly relevant to a combination intended for allergic rhinitis.

Neuropsychiatric events have been reported in adults, adolescents and children taking montelukast. Patients and caregivers should be instructed to notify their physician if such changes occur, and prescribers should carefully evaluate the risks and benefits of continuing treatment if they do.
Montelukast must not be used to treat an acute asthma attack. Patients should be advised to keep their usual rescue medication, a short-acting inhaled beta-agonist, available.
Montelukast should not be substituted abruptly for inhaled or oral corticosteroids, and there is no evidence that oral corticosteroids can be reduced when montelukast is added.

Rarely, patients on anti-asthma agents including montelukast develop systemic eosinophilia with features of vasculitis consistent with Churg-Strauss syndrome, sometimes following a reduction in corticosteroid dose. Physicians should watch for eosinophilia, vasculitic rash, worsening pulmonary symptoms, cardiac complications or neuropathy.

Caution is advised with levocetirizine in patients with factors predisposing to urinary retention, such as spinal cord lesion or prostatic hyperplasia, and in patients with epilepsy, because seizures may be aggravated.

Although levocetirizine does not impair driving at recommended doses, some patients may experience somnolence, fatigue or asthenia, and should assess their own response before driving or using machines. Caution is recommended with concurrent alcohol intake.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to levocetirizine, to cetirizine, to hydroxyzine, to any piperazine derivative, to montelukast, or to any of the excipients.
End-stage renal disease with an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 15 millilitres per minute, requiring dialysis, which contraindicates levocetirizine.
The levocetirizine film-coated tablet presentation is not recommended for children under 6 years of age.
interactions: Concurrent administration of levocetirizine with alcohol or other central nervous system depressants may cause additional reductions in alertness and impairment of performance.
Ritonavir increased exposure to cetirizine, the racemate of levocetirizine, by approximately 40 per cent.
Theophylline produced a small decrease of about 16 per cent in levocetirizine clearance.

Phenobarbital decreased the area under the curve of montelukast by approximately 40 per cent, and concurrent use of the enzyme inducers phenytoin, phenobarbital and rifampicin should be avoided without careful monitoring.

Gemfibrozil, an inhibitor of CYP2C8 and CYP2C9, increased systemic exposure to montelukast 4.4-fold. No routine dose adjustment is required, but physicians should watch for increased adverse reactions.
clinical.scopeNote: Assembled from two single-ingredient UK Summaries of Product Characteristics because no combination licence was located in a major jurisdiction. Both sources match the strengths in this product, a levocetirizine 5 mg film-coated tablet and a montelukast 10 mg film-coated tablet, but they describe two separate tablets taken on their own rather than a single fixed combination. The montelukast source's date of last revision is November 2019, which is older than the other sources cited here. UK montelukast labelling covers asthma as add-on therapy and, only in asthmatic patients, symptomatic relief of seasonal allergic rhinitis; it does not support use for allergic rhinitis in patients without asthma, and that mismatch with a levocetirizine-based combination has not been resolved by any source reviewed here. The US Food and Drug Administration required a boxed warning on montelukast in March 2020 and advised that it be prescribed for allergic rhinitis only in patients with an inadequate response or intolerance to alternative therapies; that advice applies to the United States and is reproduced here as regulatory context, not as a statement of this product's Indian licensing status. Nothing above verifies KRUJOCET-M's India-approved indication, its pack insert, or the clinical effect of the specific 5 mg / 10 mg combination.

clinical.summary: Ramnova modified-release capsule containing enteric-coated pantoprazole sodium and sustained-release domperidone. The strength of each ingredient requires packaging confirmation and is not stated here. No combination-product licence was located in a major regulatory jurisdiction, so the outline below is drawn from the UK Summary of Product Characteristics for each ingredient separately. Note that UK labelling for domperidone covers only the relief of nausea and vomiting, limits adults to 30 mg per day, and limits treatment to a maximum of one week. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: UK labelling for pantoprazole covers reflux oesophagitis in adults and in adolescents aged 12 years and above.

UK labelling for pantoprazole in adults also covers gastric and duodenal ulcer, eradication of Helicobacter pylori in combination with appropriate antibiotic therapy, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome together with other pathological hypersecretory conditions.
UK labelling for domperidone covers only the relief of the symptoms of nausea and vomiting. Indications relating to dyspepsia, heartburn and reflux were not present in the labelling reviewed.
sideEffects: Common with pantoprazole are headache, dizziness, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension and bloating, and constipation.
Serious manifestations of hypomagnesaemia such as fatigue, tetany, delirium and convulsions may occur with prolonged proton pump inhibitor use.

Proton pump inhibitors are associated with very infrequent cases of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and with severe cutaneous adverse reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Common with domperidone are somnolence and headache.
Domperidone has been associated with prolongation of the QT interval and with rare cases of torsades de pointes.
warnings: A symptomatic response to pantoprazole may mask the signs of gastric malignancy, and investigation should be undertaken if symptoms persist despite adequate treatment.
Proton pump inhibitors may modestly increase the risk of hip, wrist and spine fracture, predominantly in the elderly.

Epidemiological studies showed that domperidone was associated with an increased risk of serious ventricular arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death. The risk is higher in patients older than 60 years, at daily doses above 30 mg, and with concurrent QT-prolonging medicines or potent CYP3A4 inhibitors.

UK labelling limits adults to a maximum domperidone dose of 30 mg per day and states that the maximum treatment duration should not exceed one week. Because this product's domperidone strength requires packaging confirmation, its relationship to that limit cannot be stated here.
Long-term pantoprazole treatment may reduce the absorption of vitamin B12, and treatment may lead to a slightly increased risk of gastrointestinal infections caused by bacteria.
Pantoprazole should be withdrawn immediately if severe cutaneous adverse reactions appear, and treatment should be stopped if lesions arise in sun-exposed areas of skin accompanied by arthralgia.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to pantoprazole, to domperidone, to substituted benzimidazoles, or to any of the excipients.
Confirmed or suspected phaeochromocytoma, or a prolactin-releasing pituitary tumour.
Gastrointestinal haemorrhage, mechanical obstruction or perforation.
Moderate or severe hepatic impairment.
Known existing prolongation of the QTc interval, significant electrolyte disturbances, or underlying cardiac disease such as congestive heart failure.
Concomitant use with QT-prolonging medicines, other than apomorphine under the specific conditions set out in its own labelling.
Concomitant use with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, regardless of their QT-prolonging effects.
interactions: Co-administration of pantoprazole with HIV protease inhibitors such as atazanavir is not recommended, because their bioavailability is significantly reduced.
Pantoprazole may interfere with the absorption of medicines whose bioavailability depends on gastric pH, such as ketoconazole.
High-dose methotrexate given with pantoprazole may increase methotrexate levels.
There have been reports of increased INR and prothrombin time in patients taking pantoprazole together with warfarin or phenprocoumon, and monitoring is required.

Concomitant use of domperidone with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, including HIV protease inhibitors, systemic azole antifungals such as ketoconazole, and macrolides such as erythromycin, is contraindicated. Marked interaction with ketoconazole or erythromycin produced mean QTc prolongation of approximately 10 milliseconds.
Concomitant use of domperidone with other QT-prolonging medicines is contraindicated, with the specific exception of apomorphine used under the precautions set out in its own labelling.

Neither ingredient strength in this product has been confirmed against the packaging, so no strength-specific statement can be made and the dose-dependent domperidone cardiac risk cannot be placed relative to the 30 mg per day limit. The pantoprazole source describes a 40 mg gastro-resistant tablet and the domperidone source a 10 mg orodispersible immediate-release tablet; neither matches the modified-release capsule presentation here. The domperidone labelled indication is limited to the relief of nausea and vomiting for no longer than one week, a limit set for that presentation and not shown here to apply unchanged to a sustained-release combination intended for longer use alongside a proton pump inhibitor. sourceDescription: Rabeprazole 20 mg + Levosulpiride 75 mg SR Capsules
displayDescription: Rabeprazole 20 mg and levosulpiride 75 mg sustained-release capsules

clinical.summary: Ramnova sustained-release capsule containing rabeprazole and levosulpiride. No combination-product licence was located in a major regulatory jurisdiction. The rabeprazole outline below is drawn from the UK Summary of Product Characteristics. No UK or US licensed product information was located for levosulpiride, so the entries for that component are drawn from published Indian clinical studies rather than from approved labelling. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: UK labelling for rabeprazole covers active duodenal ulcer and active benign gastric ulcer, erosive or ulcerative gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and long-term management of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

UK labelling for rabeprazole also covers symptomatic treatment of moderate to very severe gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and eradication of Helicobacter pylori in combination with appropriate antibacterial therapy.

No approved indication for levosulpiride was located in UK or US labelling. Published Indian clinical literature describes it as a substituted benzamide used increasingly for gastric motility disorders, and commonly prescribed alongside proton pump inhibitors.
sideEffects: Common with rabeprazole are headache, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, asthenia, flatulence, rash and dry mouth.
Severe hypomagnesaemia has been reported in patients treated with proton pump inhibitors for at least three months.
Proton pump inhibitors are associated with very infrequent cases of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and with erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Levosulpiride has been associated with movement disorders. In a prospective study of 30 patients at an Indian tertiary care centre, 86.66 per cent presented with stiffness, tremor or both; reported features included resting tremor, rigidity, dystonia, dysarthria, abnormal gait, and neck or back pain with muscle spasm.

Levosulpiride raises serum prolactin. A published Indian case report describes a patient taking levosulpiride sustained release 75 mg who developed a serum prolactin of 273 nanograms per millilitre against a reference range of 3.7 to 17.9, with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea; the authors note that a significant number of patients who use levosulpiride develop levels above 200 nanograms per millilitre, and cite a study reporting galactorrhoea in 26.7 per cent of patients.
warnings: A symptomatic response to rabeprazole does not preclude the presence of gastric or oesophageal malignancy, and malignancy should therefore be excluded before treatment begins.
Proton pump inhibitors may modestly increase the risk of hip, wrist and spine fracture, predominantly in the elderly.

Levosulpiride-induced movement disorders became more frequent with longer treatment. In the Indian study cited, onset ranged from four days to more than six months, most patients presented after three to five weeks, and a statistically significant positive correlation was found between treatment duration and the incidence of tremor and stiffness.

The authors of that study advise that levosulpiride should be considered as a possible cause of acute recent-onset extrapyramidal syndromes, and that early recognition is essential for complete recovery.
In the prolactin case reported, serum prolactin fell and menstruation resumed within one to two weeks of stopping levosulpiride, which indicates that the effect may be reversible on withdrawal.
Rabeprazole may reduce the absorption of vitamin B12 as a consequence of hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria, which may be relevant during long-term treatment.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to rabeprazole, to levosulpiride, to substituted benzimidazoles, or to any of the excipients.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding, which the rabeprazole labelling reviewed lists as contraindications.

No licensed contraindication list was located for levosulpiride in a major regulatory jurisdiction. The absence of a listed set of contraindications is not evidence that none apply, and the pack insert should be consulted.
interactions: Proton pump inhibitors including rabeprazole should not be co-administered with atazanavir, because exposure to atazanavir is reduced.
Rabeprazole may cause a significant decrease in the plasma levels of antifungals whose absorption depends on gastric pH, such as ketoconazole and itraconazole.
Concomitant use of rabeprazole with methotrexate may elevate and prolong serum levels of methotrexate and its metabolite.
Rabeprazole is metabolised by CYP2C19, and slow metabolisers show an increased area under the curve and half-life compared with extensive metabolisers.

No licensed interaction profile was located for levosulpiride in a major regulatory jurisdiction. Because levosulpiride acts as a dopamine D2 antagonist, the pack insert should be consulted before use with other dopamine antagonists or with dopaminergic medicines.
clinical.scopeNote: No combination licence was located in a major jurisdiction. The rabeprazole entries come from a UK Summary of Product Characteristics for a 20 mg gastro-resistant tablet, matching the strength in this product; its date of last revision is December 2017, which is older than the other sources cited here. Levosulpiride holds no UK or US marketing authorisation, so no approved labelling exists for it; the entries above are drawn from two peer-reviewed Indian publications, one a prospective single-centre study of 30 patients and the other a single case report with a literature discussion. Those are observational reports of harm rather than regulatory labelling, and they do not constitute a complete adverse-effect, contraindication or interaction profile. The prolactin case report concerns levosulpiride sustained release 75 mg, which matches the levosulpiride strength in this product. Nothing above verifies RUSKIRAB-L's India-approved indication, its pack insert, or the clinical effect of the specific 20 mg / 75 mg SR combination.

name: SIZEDOB
displayDescription: Calcium dobesilate monohydrate capsules

clinical.summary: Ramnova capsule listed as calcium dobesilate monohydrate, with no strength stated. Calcium dobesilate is a licensed medicine in several European and Latin American countries but not in the United Kingdom or the United States. No Indian pack insert or CDSCO approval for this product was located, so the outline below is drawn from the Spanish regulatory ficha tecnica for a licensed calcium dobesilate 500 mg capsule. That label carries a very rare but serious warning about agranulocytosis. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: The Spanish label for calcium dobesilate 500 mg hard capsules lists a single indication, non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
The label does not list chronic venous insufficiency or haemorrhoids as indications for this presentation, although calcium dobesilate is used for those conditions in some other countries.
sideEffects: Frequent gastrointestinal effects are nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and abdominal pain.
Headache is frequent.
Joint pain and muscle pain are frequent.
Raised alanine aminotransferase is frequent.
Infrequent effects are fever, chills, weakness and fatigue.
Infrequent hypersensitivity effects are rash, allergic dermatitis, itching, hives and facial oedema.
Anaphylactic reaction is very rare.
Agranulocytosis, leukopenia and neutropenia are reported at a frequency the label does not establish.
warnings: In very rare cases calcium dobesilate can induce agranulocytosis, which may present only as the non-specific symptoms of an infection.

Patients should be told that if they develop symptoms suggesting infection, such as fever or inflammation of the mucous membranes of the palate, tonsils or tongue, they must inform their doctor immediately. A blood count including a white cell count should then be performed and treatment should be stopped.
Severe hypersensitivity reactions have been reported.
Calcium dobesilate interferes with enzymatic creatinine assays and can produce falsely low creatinine values. Blood samples for laboratory testing should be taken before the first dose of the day.
A dose reduction may be needed in patients with severe renal impairment requiring dialysis.

The Spanish label advises against use during pregnancy, despite no harmful effects having been seen in animal studies. Calcium dobesilate is excreted in breast milk in small amounts, and as a precaution either treatment or breastfeeding should be discontinued.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to calcium dobesilate or to any of the excipients.
interactions: Calcium dobesilate may interfere with the enzymatic measurement of creatinine, producing falsely low values, so blood samples should be collected before the first daily dose. No other interaction is listed in the source label.
clinical.scopeNote: Drawn from one Spanish regulatory ficha tecnica for a licensed calcium dobesilate 500 mg hard capsule, because no Indian pack insert, CDSCO approval or Indian peer-reviewed source for SIZEDOB itself was located, and calcium dobesilate has no United Kingdom or United States licence to fall back on. Three gaps are unresolved. First, this product does not state a strength anywhere in the listing, and the product record flags that for packaging confirmation; the source label describes a 500 mg capsule taken as 1500 to 2000 mg daily in two divided doses, so nothing above can be read as a dose for SIZEDOB. Second, the indication does not match the catalogue positioning: the source label lists only non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, whereas this product is categorised under vascular care, and that therapy category is itself marked as inferred from composition rather than sourced. Calcium dobesilate is used for chronic venous disease and haemorrhoids in some countries, but the label cited here does not support those uses for this presentation and no source reviewed here establishes an Indian approved indication. Third, the source label carries a date of revision of June 2017, which is older than most sources used elsewhere in this catalogue, and it describes a Spanish product with its own excipients, not this one. Nothing above verifies the strength, dosing, excipients or India-approved indication of SIZEDOB.

name: SIZEHEM-XT
displayDescription: Ferrous ascorbate and folic acid tablets

clinical.summary: Ramnova tablet listed as ferrous ascorbate with folic acid, with no strength stated for either ingredient. No Indian pack insert or CDSCO approval for this combination was located, so the outline below is drawn from UK Summaries of Product Characteristics for a licensed oral iron tablet and for folic acid tablets separately. Two points carry over strongly: iron overdose can be fatal in young children, and folic acid should not be given without adequate vitamin B12 in people whose B12 status is untreated or unknown. This product contains folic acid and no vitamin B12. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: UK labelling for an oral ferrous salt tablet covers iron-deficiency anaemia.

UK labelling for folic acid covers the treatment of megaloblastic anaemia due to folic acid deficiency, and prophylaxis in chronic haemolytic states, renal dialysis and drug-induced folate deficiency, as well as prevention of recurrence of neural tube defects.
sideEffects: Common effects of oral iron are abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, constipation and diarrhoea.
Oral iron darkens the stools.
Gastrointestinal effects reported with folic acid include abdominal distension, flatulence, anorexia and nausea.
Allergic reactions to folic acid are rare and include erythema, rash, urticaria, dyspnoea and anaphylaxis.
warnings: The source iron labelling carries the warning that the product contains iron and must be kept out of the sight and reach of children, because overdose may be fatal. Overdosage of ferrous salts is particularly dangerous to young children.

Folic acid should not be given for pernicious anaemia or undiagnosed megaloblastic anaemia without sufficient vitamin B12, because folic acid alone will not prevent and may precipitate subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. This product contains folic acid and does not contain vitamin B12, so this warning applies directly to it, and the source labelling treats long-term folate in untreated cobalamin deficiency as a contraindication.
Caution is required with folic acid in patients with folate-dependent tumours.
Caution is advised with oral iron in patients with a history of peptic ulcer, inflammatory bowel disease, intestinal strictures or diverticular disease.
The source iron labelling states that dental caries is a definite risk with long-term treatment, and that tablets should be swallowed whole to avoid mouth ulceration and tooth discoloration.
Iron should not be taken orally and parenterally at the same time.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to the active substances or excipients.
Haemochromatosis and haemosiderosis.
Repeated blood transfusions.
Haemolytic anaemia, and anaemia not due to iron deficiency.
Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.
Active peptic ulcer.
Regional enteritis and ulcerative colitis.
For the folic acid component, malignant disease, unless there is megaloblastic anaemia due to folic acid deficiency.
Concurrent use of oral and parenteral iron.
interactions: Iron reduces the absorption of tetracycline antibiotics, and the source labelling advises separating doses by two to three hours.
Iron reduces the absorption of quinolone antibiotics, levothyroxine, bisphosphonates and trientine, with a separation of at least two hours advised.
Iron reduces the absorption of penicillamine, mycophenolate mofetil and dopaminergic medicines such as levodopa and methyldopa.
Antacids, calcium salts and zinc impair the absorption of iron.
Sulfasalazine and cholestyramine reduce folic acid absorption, and antacids reduce it unless dosing is separated by at least two hours.
Trimethoprim and sulfonamides reduce the effectiveness of folic acid.
Serum levels of the anticonvulsants phenytoin, phenobarbital and primidone may be reduced by folic acid.
Folic acid may reduce the intestinal absorption of zinc.
clinical.scopeNote: Assembled from two UK Summaries of Product Characteristics, one for an oral ferrous salt tablet and one for folic acid tablets, because no Indian pack insert, CDSCO approval or Indian peer-reviewed source for SIZEHEM-XT itself was located. Several gaps are unresolved. Neither ingredient has a stated strength in the product listing, and the product record flags both for packaging confirmation, so nothing above can be read as a dose and the folic acid content cannot be compared with the 5 mg tablet that the folic acid source describes. The iron salt also differs: this product is listed as ferrous ascorbate, whereas the iron source describes ferrous sulfate, which provides about 65 mg of elemental iron per 200 mg tablet. Ferrous ascorbate and ferrous sulfate differ in elemental iron content per milligram, and ascorbate is present partly because ascorbic acid affects iron absorption; no source reviewed here characterises the ferrous ascorbate presentation, its elemental iron content, or its tolerability relative to ferrous sulfate. Some contraindications listed above, such as active peptic ulcer and ulcerative colitis, come from the specific ferrous sulfate label cited and may not appear on every oral iron label. The folic acid source carries a date of revision of July 2018, which is older than the iron source. name: SILIRAM-MAX
displayDescription: Silymarin, L-ornithine L-aspartate, tricholine citrate and multivitamin syrup

clinical.summary: Ramnova syrup listed as silymarin with L-ornithine L-aspartate, tricholine citrate and an unenumerated multivitamin blend. No strength is stated for any ingredient. The two components that can be sourced both have negative or inconclusive evidence: a United States evidence review reports that trials of silymarin in hepatitis C and in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis did not show benefit, and a Cochrane review concluded that evidence is insufficient to confidently recommend L-ornithine L-aspartate for preventing or managing hepatic encephalopathy. Refer to the current pack insert and a qualified healthcare professional for complete prescribing information.
uses: The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health reports that study results for milk thistle in liver disease have been conflicting or too limited to allow conclusions, and that two trials it funded, one in hepatitis C and one in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, did not show benefits from supplementation with the milk thistle extract silymarin.
The same review notes that a small number of studies in people suggest milk thistle extracts may help control blood sugar in people with type 2 diabetes.

A Cochrane review of L-ornithine L-aspartate in people with cirrhosis concluded that the evidence is insufficient to confidently recommend it for preventing or managing hepatic encephalopathy, with certainty of evidence rated very low to low.
No source reviewed here establishes a use for this product or for this combination of ingredients.
sideEffects: Reported effects of milk thistle are digestive symptoms such as bloating, nausea and gas.
Allergic reactions to milk thistle may occur, particularly in people allergic to related plants such as ragweed, chrysanthemum, marigold and daisy.
warnings: The cited review notes a product-quality concern specific to milk thistle: some products have been found to contain amounts of silymarin substantially different from the label, or to be contaminated with pesticides, microorganisms or mycotoxins. The silymarin content of this product is not stated and is not verified by any source reviewed here.
Because milk thistle extracts may affect blood sugar control in people with type 2 diabetes, anyone using glucose-lowering treatment should raise this with a health professional before use.
People allergic to ragweed, chrysanthemum, marigold or daisy may react to milk thistle.

The Cochrane review of L-ornithine L-aspartate assessed it in people with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy, a hospital population under specialist care. Nothing in that review supports use of the ingredient outside that setting, and it notes considerable risk of bias in the included trials and evidence of small-study effects.
interactions: No specific drug interaction is named for milk thistle in the cited review, which advises anyone taking any type of medicine to consult a health professional before use.
No interaction statement for L-ornithine L-aspartate, tricholine citrate or the multivitamin blend is established by any source reviewed here.
clinical.scopeNote: Assembled from one United States evidence review and one Cochrane systematic review, because no Indian pack insert, CDSCO approval or Indian peer-reviewed source for SILIRAM-MAX was located. The gaps are extensive. No strength is stated for any of the four listed components, and the multivitamin blend is not itemised anywhere reviewed here, so nothing above can be read as a dose and no vitamin can be checked against a recommended intake or an upper intake level. Tricholine citrate is named in the composition but is not covered by any source cited here, and no claim is made about it. The silymarin source is a general evidence and safety summary about milk thistle; it does not correspond to any particular extract, standardisation or dose, and it is not regulatory labelling. The L-ornithine L-aspartate source is a systematic review in people with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy, which is a different population and a different level of care from anyone likely to be given a syrup on general liver support grounds; its conclusion is cited for what it says about the ingredient, not as evidence about this product, and specific trial counts and effect estimates from it are deliberately not reproduced here because they could not be read reliably from the copy consulted. Neither source addresses the combination of silymarin with L-ornithine L-aspartate, and no source reviewed here explains why the two are combined with a choline salt and vitamins in one syrup. The contraindications list is empty because neither cited source is a regulatory label and neither establishes a contraindication. The catalogue therapy category, liver and nutritional support, is itself marked as inferred from composition rather than sourced. Nothing above verifies the India-approved status, composition, strengths, dosing or pack insert of SILIRAM-MAX.
